question: A 17-year-old girl comes to the physician because of a 3-year history of acne on her face and chest. She has no itching or scaling. She is concerned about the possibility of facial scarring and has never sought treatment. She has no history of serious illness. She takes no medications. She is 160 cm (5 ft 3 in) tall and weighs 58 kg (130 lb); BMI is 23 kg/m2. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows several open comedones on the face and chest. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

A 17-year-old girl comes to the physician because of a 3-year history of acne on her face and chest. She has no itching or scaling. She is concerned about the possibility of facial scarring and has never sought treatment. She has no history of serious illness. She takes no medications. She is 160 cm (5 ft 3 in) tall and weighs 58 kg (130 lb); BMI is 23 kg/m2. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows several open comedones on the face and chest. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

A. Oral antibiotics
B. Topical benzoyl peroxide
C. Topical antibiotic
D. Oral isotretinoin

# Reasoning

General comment Only one trial looks specifically at patients with comedonal acne. As a source of indirect evidence, trials including patients with papulopustular acne were used and the percentage in the reduction of non-inflammatory lesions was

considered as the relevant outcome parameter. Because of the general lack of direct evidence for the treatment of comedonal acne, the strength of recommendation was downgraded for all considered treatment options, starting with medium strength of recommendation as a maximum.

Due to the usually mild to moderate severity of comedonal acne, generally, a topical therapy is recommended.

The best efficacy was shown for topical retinoids, BPO and azelaic acid.

The tolerability of topical retinoids and BPO is comparable; there is a trend towards azelaic acid having a better safety/tolerability profile than BPO and a comparable profile to adapalene (indirect evidence, see Table 11 in long version).

The fixed-dose combination of adapalene with BPO shows a trend towards better efficacy against non-inflammatory lesions (NIL) when compared to BPO and a comparable efficacy when compared to adapalene (see Table 4 in long version). However, there is also a trend towards inferiority of the fixed combination with respect to the safety/tolerability profile (indirect evidence, see Table 12 in long version).

The fixed-dose combinations of clindamycin with BPO showed a trend towards better efficacy against NIL vs. clindamycin and comparable efficacy vs. BPO (see Table 5 in long version). With respect to the safety/tolerability profile, the combination is comparable to its single components (indirect evidence, see Table 12 in long version).

Few and only indirect data on patient preference are available. They indicate patient preference for adapalene over other topical retinoids.

Additional pathophysiological considerations favour the use of topical retinoids (reduction of microcomedones).

# Clinical question 2: At what ages is treatment indicated?

According to EMA, isotretinoin is not indicated for the treatment of prepubertal acne and is not recommended in patients $< 12$ years of age. The European guidelines are conformed with these recommendations; however, experts agreed that an age under 12 years does not exclude obligatorily isotretinoin administration.[15]

Evidence-based recommendations for paediatric acne were published in 2013. The consensus article recommended isotretinoin for severe, scarring and/or refractory acne in adolescents (strength of recommendation A: based on consistent and good-quality patient-oriented evidence) and stated that it may be used in younger patients (strength of recommendation C: based on consensus, usual practice, opinion, disease-oriented evidence or case series for studies of diagnosis, treatment, prevention or screening).<sup>18</sup> It was also recommended to provide extensive counselling on isotretinoin teratogenicity and pregnancy avoidance and to monitor carefully for possible adverse events.<sup>18</sup> It was noted that the majority of clinical trials for acne medications are conducted in patients 12 years of age or older, and there is not sufficient evidence for acne treatments in paediatric patients<sup>18</sup> (Table 2).

# Clinical question 9: What are the recommendations for preventing acne flares during isotretinoin treatment?

A flare (exacerbation) of acne may occur in up to $15\%$ of acne patients during the initial period of isotretinoin intake.[17,54] The topic of acne flares and how to prevent them is inconsistently addressed across guidelines and consensus articles (Table 3).

According to the French guidelines, comedone extraction may be proposed before isotretinoin onset in order to decrease the risk of severe inflammatory flares at treatment initiation (expert consensus). For numerous and very severe comedones, isotretinoin should also be initiated at a lower dose of $0.2-0.3\mathrm{mg/kg/day}$ in order to decrease the risk of acute and severe exacerbation (acne fulminans) (expert consensus) (Table 1).

In the consensus articles of Thiboutot et al. and Eichenfield et al., it is recommended to start with a low dose $(0.5\mathrm{mg / kg})$ for the first 4 weeks to avoid initial flares and then increasing to the full dosage of $1\mathrm{mg / kg}$ per day.[17]

# Recommendations for comedonal acne

High strength of recommendation

None

Medium strength of recommendation

Topical retinoids ${}^{2}$ can be recommended for the treatment of comedonal acne.

Low strength of recommendation

Azelaic acid can be considered for the treatment of comedonal acne. BPO can be considered for the treatment of comedonal acne.

Open recommendation

A recommendation for or against treatment of comedonal acne with visible light as monotherapy, lasers with visible wavelengths and lasers with infrared wavelengths, with intense pulsed light (IPL) and photodynamic therapy (PDT) cannot be made at the present time.

Negative recommendation

Topical antibiotics are not recommended for the treatment of comedonal acne.

Hormonal anti-androgens, systemic antibiotics and/or systemic isotretinoin are not recommended for the treatment of comedonal acne.

Artificial ultraviolet (UV) radiation is not recommended for the treatment of comedonal acne.

1 Limitations can apply that may necessitate the use of a treatment with a lower strength of recommendation as a first line therapy (e.g. financial resources/reimbursement limitations, legal restrictions, availability, drug licensing).   
$^{2}$ Adapalene to be preferred over tretinoin/isotretinoin (see chapter 5.4.1 in long version).

# Further evidence

Similarly, a recent systematic review mentioned that all published randomized controlled trials for isotretinoin in acne included patients older than 12 years of age.[8]

Acne may present at an earlier age than 12 years, including neonates, infants, mid-childhood or prepubertal children. However, acne in these younger age groups is not usually severe to require oral isotretinoin. Neonatal acne is a self-limiting condition, infantile acne usually responds to topical anti-acne agents or systemic antibiotics for more severe types, acne in mid-childhood (between 1 and 7 years of age) is very rare and hyperandrogenism should always be ruled out.[23] Rare patients with recalcitrant infantile acne associated with scarring that needed isotretinoin have been reported. It is outside the scope of this review to discuss in detail these cases that have been reviewed elsewhere.[23]

A limitation in the prescribing indication of isotretinoin by EMA is the definition of 'puberty' at age 12. Acne in prepubertal age may be the first physical sign of pubertal maturation, and thus, the presence of severe acne should raise a suspicion of possible endocrine disorders such as premature adrenarche, congenital adrenal hyperplasia or true precocious puberty.[24-26] A retrospective US study in the National Ambulatory Medical Care Survey database over the period from 1979 to 2007 reported a significant decrease in the mean age of children seeking treatment for acne. They reported that these results support the increasingly earlier onset of puberty in children.[27]

# General considerations

Choice of type of topical retinoid

Adapalene should be selected in preference to tretinoin and isotretinoin.

Choice of type of systemic antibiotic

Doxycycline and lymecycline should be selected in preference to minocycline and tetracycline.

Considerations on isotretinoin and dosage

For severe papulopustular acne/moderate nodular acne, a dosage of systemic isotretinoin of $0.3 - 0.5\mathrm{mg / kg}$ can be recommended.

For conglobate acne a dosage of systemic isotretinoin of $\geq 0.5\mathrm{mg / kg}$ can be recommended.

The duration of the therapy should be at least 6 months.

In case of insufficient response, the treatment period can be prolonged.
